name: Creative Marketing Agency Capabilities Deck
description: An editorial creative-agency credentials deck in warm ivory, near black, and coral red for presenting a differentiated agency point of view, modular services, selected case studies, attributable commercial proof, engagement models, and a direct path to partnership.
style_guide:
# Editorial Creative Marketing Agency Capabilities Deck

## Design intent

Create a capabilities deck that demonstrates how an agency thinks, what it can credibly deliver, where it has created value, how clients can engage it, and what should happen next. The deck should feel like a carefully edited credentials portfolio rather than a catalog of disciplines or a montage of campaign images. Its strongest asset is a clear point of view expressed through editorial typography, precise claims, selective proof, and generous space.

Use warm ivory as the dominant paper-like surface, near black for authority, and coral red as the single brand signal. The system combines expressive serif headlines and italic phrases with practical sans-serif evidence. It should feel contemporary, premium, and commercially literate without becoming ornamental.

The preview images define composition and visual tone only. Do not reuse the preview agency, domain, client names, projects, services, people, contact details, dates, commercial models, metrics, testimonials, or outcomes. Build all content from the current workspace and visibly label concept work, examples, estimates, self-reported results, and placeholders.

## Core visual signature

- Carry a narrow coral-red rail along the far left of every page. It is the strongest persistent identity element and may bleed to the canvas edge.
- Use a warm-ivory full-page surface with almost no decorative imagery. Structure comes from type, spacing, thin rules, alignment, and occasional white evidence panels.
- Lead each page with a large editorial serif conclusion. Highlight one short phrase in coral italic to create voice and contrast.
- Place a compact red section label at upper left and a neutral gray context label at upper right.
- Use black serif for the agency thesis, service names, case titles, quotations, and partnership model names. Use sans serif for descriptions, proof, metadata, and operational detail.
- Preserve a quiet lower frame with agency or deck label at left and a two-digit page counter at right.
- Prefer one strong composition per page: thesis plus differentiators, three services, two cases, three proof points, or three engagement models.

## Canvas, grid, and spacing

- Author on a fixed 1920 × 1080, 16:9 canvas.
- Reserve approximately 48 px for the persistent left coral rail. Keep essential content at least 116–136 px from the left edge and 100–120 px from the right edge.
- Keep the upper metadata line around 92–112 px from the top. Place the main headline between 170 and 305 px depending on its length.
- Use a 12-column grid with 20–26 px gutters. Align headline, body statement, card edges, metric baselines, footer label, and page counter.
- Use 32–48 px between major regions, 20–28 px between cards, and 14–20 px inside related text groups.
- Preserve at least 20 percent open space on ordinary pages. Remove weak proof or split the page rather than compressing the editorial rhythm.
- Use thin one-pixel rules and square or nearly square panels. Corners should be 0–4 px. Avoid visible shadows.
- Keep body copy at 18–23 px, card copy at 16–21 px, labels at 12–15 px, and page conclusions at 54–78 px.

## Color system

### Primary palette

- Warm ivory: #F7F5F0. Dominant canvas, editorial field, and document surface.
- Near black: #11110F. Main headline, body copy, table headings, and strongest evidence.
- Coral red: #DD3E38. Persistent rail, italic phrase, section label, case number, metric, active rule, and call to action.
- Clean white: #FFFFFF. Service, case, proof, and engagement panels when separation from ivory is needed.
- Warm gray: #68635D. Upper-right context, captions, explanatory copy, and secondary metadata.
- Rule beige: #DEDAD3. Panel border, divider, table rule, and inactive structure.
- Soft coral tint: #FFF1EF. Testimonial field, after state, selected model, or gentle action band.

### Semantic exceptions

- Verified positive green: #267A4D only for an independently verified positive status where a case-study chart requires it.
- Risk amber: #A76A18 only for a constraint, unresolved dependency, or commercial caveat.
- Client campaign colors may appear inside a clearly bounded and labeled client artifact. They must not leak into the agency master frame.
- Coral red is an identity and attention color, not a universal positive or negative status.
- Never rely on color alone. Pair state with text, value, rule, or position.

## Typography

- Use DM Serif Display, Source Serif 4, Georgia, or another high-contrast editorial serif for cover statements, page conclusions, service names, case titles, metrics, quotations, and engagement-model names.
- Use Inter, Helvetica Neue, Arial, or another neutral grotesk for descriptions, evidence, bullet lists, labels, case details, commercial terms, and next steps.
- Use IBM Plex Mono, Roboto Mono, or another restrained mono face only for project IDs, dates, evidence windows, page counts, or compact technical metadata when needed.
- Use serif italic to emphasize one short strategic or emotive phrase per page. Do not italicize complete paragraphs or every red phrase.
- Cover and page conclusions may be 58–80 px with a line height around 1.0–1.08. Service and case titles may be 30–40 px. Key metrics may be 50–72 px.
- Use sans-serif labels at 12–15 px with moderate tracking. Body copy should remain 18–23 px with a line height of 1.4–1.55.
- Use sentence case for arguments. Reserve all caps for short section labels, categories, proof status, and footer metadata.
- Do not use more than one serif and one sans-serif family in the core system.

## Persistent frame

- Keep the coral rail at a fixed width and position throughout the deck.
- Place a two-digit section number and short topic at upper left in coral red.
- Place a quiet purpose or audience cue at upper right in warm gray.
- Place agency or deck name at lower left and page count at lower right.
- Use stable terminology: point of view, capability, service, client problem, idea, execution, role, result, evidence, engagement, scope, cadence, team, next step.
- Keep the same headline measure, card borders, label style, and footer baseline across all pages.
- Client-specific colors, logos, and visuals must remain inside case-study panels and must never replace the agency frame.

## Page archetypes

### Cover and capabilities portfolio

Use a very open ivory page with the coral rail, a small capabilities label, organization and period context, one large editorial value proposition, a compact capability index, agency name, presentation purpose, presenter or contact, date, and confidentiality status where appropriate. The headline should state the agency's commercial or cultural promise rather than claim vague creativity. Do not use a montage of work on the cover.

### Agency positioning and differentiators

Use an asymmetric thesis-and-proof composition. State the gap the agency is built to close, define the ideal partner or situation, and explain the operating belief in one short paragraph. On the right, show three or four differentiators using the same fields: method, client consequence, evidence, and boundary. Avoid empty attributes such as bold, integrated, disruptive, or full service.

### Services and working models

Show no more than three primary service pillars. Each pillar should identify the client problem, work performed, typical outputs, collaboration model, core team, duration or cadence, dependencies, and what is explicitly out of scope. Distinguish capabilities delivered in-house from partner-supported production, media, technology, research, localization, or specialist work. Make modularity visible without implying that every client needs every service.

### Selected case studies and impact

Use two substantial cases rather than a wall of logos. Apply a consistent structure: client context, challenge, insight or idea, execution, agency role, partner role, result, measurement basis, and evidence date. Before-and-after fields may show the strategic change, but they must not oversimplify multi-factor outcomes. If client permission is limited, anonymize accurately and state the limitation.

### Client proof and business results

Use up to three large metrics plus one attributable testimonial or a clearly labeled synthesis of multiple interviews. Define every metric's unit, period, baseline, attribution method, and source. Separate brand outcomes, media outcomes, engagement, pipeline, sales, realized revenue, retention, lifetime value, and return on spend. A result that cannot be causally attributed should be framed as associated, contributed, or directional.

### Engagement models and next steps

Present two or three ways to work together, such as a retained partnership, defined project, sprint, embedded team, or performance-linked structure. For each, show scope, cadence, team shape, client responsibilities, duration, commercial basis, best fit, exclusions, and decision gate. Close with a short discovery-to-proposal-to-kickoff route, named owners, expected timing, and a direct next action.

## Agency and client evidence integrity

- Preview content is fictional visual reference. Never copy preview agency names, clients, case studies, metrics, contact details, dates, services, testimonials, pricing, or results.
- Never invent clients, logos, project roles, campaign reach, impressions, earned media, brand lift, pipeline, revenue, conversion, return on ad spend, retention, awards, or testimonial language.
- Distinguish live work, concept work, pitch work, pro bono work, partner-led work, subcontracted work, and speculative work.
- Obtain permission before using a client name, logo, image, quotation, confidential brief, unreleased work, performance result, or identifiable stakeholder.
- State the agency's exact role. Do not imply ownership of strategy, media, production, technology, or results delivered by the client or another partner.
- Define all commercial metrics. Pipeline delivered, influenced pipeline, sourced revenue, attributed revenue, booked revenue, and realized revenue are different.
- Give every case result a baseline, measurement window, source, geography, cohort, currency, and attribution note where relevant.
- Do not compare campaign results across unlike objectives, audiences, spend levels, channels, periods, or attribution models without qualification.
- Industry benchmarks require a current source and a matched definition. Do not call an internal average an industry average.
- Testimonials require accurate wording, speaker identity, role, organization, relationship, date, and permission. When unavailable, summarize a theme without quotation marks.
- Awards and certifications require the exact awarding body, category, year, status, and current validity.
- Service claims must match actual team capacity and partner network. Do not present planned hiring or a freelance contact as an established in-house capability.
- Team biographies, tenure, credentials, and availability must be current. Avoid implying that former employees or unavailable collaborators are assigned to the engagement.
- Commercial models must state whether figures are fixed fee, time and materials, retainer, media commission, production markup, license, performance fee, revenue share, or illustrative.
- Any performance-linked fee requires verified definitions, data access, attribution, exclusions, legal review, and a dispute process.
- If evidence is missing, omit the claim, ask a visible question, or label the content as illustrative, directional, self-reported, or to be confirmed.

## Case-study and proof design

- Use white or soft-coral panels on the ivory field. Give each case a clear title, sector or work type, and compact challenge-to-impact structure.
- Keep before and after fields parallel in width and wording. Use a gray rule for the challenge and a coral rule for the changed state.
- Place one or two decisive metrics below the narrative rather than scattering values through body copy.
- Use a client artifact only when it materially proves the idea or execution. Include a caption, date, channel, and permission status.
- Do not crop work so tightly that the audience cannot understand its context, or enlarge low-resolution assets.
- Quantitative proof should be accompanied by a source or methodology note. Qualitative proof should identify whose observation it represents.
- A testimonial field may use soft coral tint and italic serif, but quotation styling does not excuse missing attribution.

## Service and engagement design

- Service pages should answer what problem is solved, what the agency does, what the client receives, who participates, and what the boundary is.
- Use no more than four bullets per service card. Bullets should be concrete deliverables or activities rather than capability synonyms.
- Engagement-model cards should be comparable. Use the same fields and ordering so a prospective client can understand tradeoffs.
- Do not mark one model recommended without a client-specific reason.
- Connect each model to a clear start sequence: discovery, brief or diagnostic, proposal, contracting, access and onboarding, kickoff.
- Show dependencies such as data access, stakeholder availability, approvals, legal review, production lead time, media budget, and technology ownership.

## Imagery and portfolio artifacts

- The default deck is typography-led. Photography and campaign work are optional evidence, not background decoration.
- When real work is available, use one large, well-captioned artifact rather than many thumbnails.
- Keep artifacts in simple rectangular frames with sufficient resolution and accurate color.
- Use mockups only when they represent delivered or explicitly labeled concept work. Do not place unfinished art into premium device mockups to imply launch.
- Avoid generic stock teams, studio desks, mood-board collages, color swatches, award statues, handshakes, megaphones, and decorative social-media grids.
- Icons are rarely necessary. If used, choose one minimal line family for service, evidence, team, timing, and next step.

## Content and narrative rules

- Each page should answer one prospective-client question: Who are you? Why are you different? What can you do? Where have you done it? What value did it create? How can we start?
- Write conclusions, not section labels. The headline should express the agency's view or the client implication.
- Keep the main deck selective. Put detailed biographies, full project lists, process maps, rate cards, references, and legal terms in an appendix or follow-up.
- Use no more than four differentiators, three service pillars, two lead cases, three proof metrics, or three engagement models on an ordinary page.
- Translate creative language into commercial or organizational consequence without pretending every creative output produces immediate revenue.
- Make the ideal client and poor-fit situation visible. Capability breadth is more credible when boundaries are explicit.
- Finish with a named next action, owner, date or time window, and required input.

## Allowed variation

- Adapt the system for brand consultancies, design studios, advertising agencies, digital-product agencies, production companies, experiential teams, media agencies, or integrated groups.
- The coral signal may be replaced with one verified agency identity color, but the single-accent discipline must remain.
- A case-study page may use a full-bleed client artifact inside the content area while preserving the coral rail and metadata frame.
- Services may be organized by client outcome, discipline, engagement stage, or industry need.
- An agency with strong visual work may use more imagery, but typography, evidence, and role clarity must remain.
- Replace serif italic emphasis with another established brand gesture only when it is part of the real agency identity.

## Avoid

- Do not reuse preview agency names, client names, project claims, numbers, testimonials, dates, contacts, or commercial terms.
- Do not fabricate recognizable client logos or imply permission through visual polish.
- Do not present concept work as launched work, pitch work as awarded work, or contributed work as solely agency-owned.
- Do not use empty superlatives, undifferentiated service lists, logo walls, award walls, or dozens of tiny portfolio images.
- Do not introduce random client colors into the agency master pages.
- Do not use coral as an unexplained positive or negative status color.
- Do not use gradients, glass effects, rounded SaaS cards, heavy shadows, 3D mockups, decorative charts, or trendy visual clutter.
- Do not claim precise business impact without source, period, basis, and attribution limits.
- Do not end with a generic contact page. End with a specific partnership route and next action.

preview_images.alt: Warm-ivory agency cover with a coral rail, bold editorial proposition, restrained category label, and spacious portfolio framing
Agency positioning page pairing a concise point of view with differentiated methods, client consequences, and proof
Three service pillars describing client problems, activities, outputs, collaboration models, and capability boundaries
Two selected case studies using a consistent challenge, idea, execution, agency role, and measurable result structure
Three quantified proof points and an attributable client testimonial or clearly labeled management synthesis
Engagement models with scope, cadence, team shape, duration, commercial basis, best fit, and a short next-step sequence
